newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico begins evacuation from still-active volcano.
newsitem.headline: Mexico begins evacuation from still-active volcano.

text.p: Mexico began evacuating residents from the slopes of the towering Popocatepetl volcano on Wednesday following a third day of explosions that spewed giant clouds of hot ash five miles (8 km) into the air.

A mudslide on the rumbling volcano's slopes shortly after the eruptions caused no deaths or injuries, but prompted officials to clear out residents in the nearby municipality of Santiago Xalitzintla, in Puebla state.
"We have evacuated residents in the upper part of the municipality in order not to put their lives in danger," Interior Minister Emilio Chuayfett told reporters.
He did not say how many people had been evacuated. Officials said they had only been moved a short distance from their homes and would be returned as soon as the danger eased.

Thousands of army troops and emergency officials were standing by to help with a larger evacuation if necessary near the 17,890-foot (5,450-meter) volcano, which lies just 33 miles (53 km) east of Mexico City, Chuayfett said.

Popocatepetl, known to Mexicans simply as "El Popo," blew a mushroom-shaped mass of gas and ash into the air on Wednesday afternoon, its biggest burst of activity since its largest eruption in 70 years on Monday.
Half a million people live dangerously close to the cone-shaped mountain, and millions more could suffer its effects were it to have a major eruption.
Scientists warned that activity within the ash and snow-covered volcano remained dangerously high.

"The volcano's activity is still quite high, although it does not compare to Monday's critical level," Alfredo Gutierrez, a spokesman for Mexico's National Centre for Disaster Prevention (Cenapred), told Reuters.
"It is too early to tell. The volcano could settle down or it could become more active," Gutierrez added, playing down fears of a massive eruption.
The volcano's last major eruption was in 1720.
Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo urged Mexicans to remain calm during a visit to Cenapred, where he watched scientists' efforts to monitor the rumbling giant.
After talking to the scientists and listening to an audio replay of Wednesday's explosions, Zedillo said all Mexicans were understandably nervous about the volcano, but urged them to remain calm.
"We want citizens to understand the government is ready to face any scenario, including that of a disaster," he said.

Monday's eruption sent hot rocks bouncing down the mountainside and blew hot ash hundreds of miles across central Mexico, spreading panic in nearby villages. Residents of Veracruz, an eastern port city 200 miles (320 km) east of the capital, dusted volcanic dust off their cars and homes.
Several villages on the flanks of the snow-capped volcano were temporarily without water on Wednesday because the ash had turned local water supply grey.
